newsitem.title: UK: Firmer mark deals blows to Norway crown and markka.
newsitem.headline: Firmer mark deals blows to Norway crown and markka.

text.p: The Nordic currencies had a tough week, except for the Danish crown, coming under pressure from a rejuvenated mark and funds selling the Norwegian crown and Finnish markka.
The markka slid to a seven-month low of 3.03 per mark on Friday and failed to gain much strength from intervention by the Bank of Finland, traders said.
Norway's crown weakened to its lowest level since late December at 4.1620 per mark.
A wave of selling by funds, reversing long positions, put both currencies under pressure.
The mark was boosted by comments late on Thursday by Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer who said the central bank was not interested in a further weakening of the German currency.

"Most European currencies are looking soggy against the mark but the Norwegian crown and the Finnish markka have had most of the impact," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy in London.

Traders said the markka's slide was surprising since the economic backdrop was positive for the currency, with economists expecting gross domestic product growth of over four percent in 1997 and continued slow inflation.

However, foreign investors build up large positions in the markka at the beginning of the year, and once they start moving out of such a relatively small market, the size of the move tends to be significant.

"There's a lot of speculative flows in that market, and once it gets going, the markka can get hit quite badly," said a trader at a Scandinavian bank in London. "Much of the weakness in the Norwegian crown spilled over into the markka," the trader said.
At 1337 GMT mark/markka was at 3.0110/40, up from 3.008/011 in late European trading on Thursday. The Norwegian crown was at 4.1265/95 against 4.1120/50.

Klaus Baader, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said the Norwegian crown had come under pressure as longs -- established in the hope that interest rates would be tightened -- were getting squeezed out.
Weak oil prices, with Brent crude trading below $18 per barrel, also weighed on the crown, said Baader.

The Swedish crown regained the upper hand versus the mark on Friday, though, on news that credit rating agency Standard and Poor's upgraded Sweden's long-term local currency credit rating to stable from negative.
Nervousness about a slightly more expansive-than- expected Swedish spring budget had weighed on the crown earlier in the week.
The Danish crown was unfazed by the Nordic nerves though, trading at 3.8093/98 compared with 3.8095/8100.
